Product strategy reading path

Brian Balfour: Zero-to-One Product Resources

A recommended reading path for going from no product to a great product.

1. The 4 Growth Frameworks You Need to Build a $100M Product

Also known as the $100M Frameworks — his flagship free essay series. Available at brianbalfour.com. This is the core sequence:

  • Market-Product Fit — start with the market (the problem), then the product (the solution), not the other way around. Define your market hypothesis using Category, Who, Problems, Motivations, then your product hypothesis using Core Value Prop, Hook, Time To Value, and Stickiness.

  • Product-Channel Fit — distribution follows a power law; most companies get zero channels to work, and if you get just one to work you have a great business.

  • Channel-Model Fit, then Model-Market Fit — the rest of the chain once you have product and channel sorted.

2. Reforge's "Product Strategy" Program

This is where Balfour (with Casey Winters and others) frames the actual work: the 5 types of product work, starting with product-market fit — going from zero to one on initial product-market fit. It's paid (Reforge membership), but it's the deepest version of the zero-to-one material if you want to go beyond the free essays.

3. "Product Work Beyond Product Market Fit" (free, Reforge blog)

Read this once you've got initial traction. The life of any company starts with going from zero to one on initial product-market fit — a requirement to reach before any other type of product work becomes a priority — but after that there are four more categories of problems: feature work, growth work, PMF expansion, and scaling work. Useful so you don't over-invest in growth tactics before PMF is real.

4. "Product Market Fit Collapse"

His piece on why PMF isn't a one-time achievement — worth reading once you think you've "arrived," since the bar keeps moving as consumer expectations rise.

Practical Order

  1. Read the $100M Frameworks essays first (free, roughly 2–3 hours).

  2. Decide if the Reforge Product Strategy course is worth the spend once you have a real product hypothesis to stress-test against it.

Note: since the fintech work already exists and aren't zero-to-one anymore, "Product Work Beyond Product Market Fit" is likely more directly useful right now than the founding-stage material.

Brian Balfour: Client & Customer Retention

Core frameworks and essays on why retention drives everything else.

Core Framework: Retention as an Output, Not an Input

Retention is fundamentally an output, with the three core inputs into retention being activation, engagement, and resurrection (reactivation). Activation isn't onboarding or education — it's getting someone all the way to establishing the habit for the first time.

Key Essay: "Retention is Hard, and Getting Harder — Here's Why"

Available on brianbalfour.com / the Reforge blog. Examines how three market dynamics — increased competition, channel fatigue, and the rise of monopolies in tech — have made retention much harder than it used to be, and digs into how each affects retention across the three stages of the user lifecycle.

Key Concept: Natural Frequency Caps Retention Potential

Retention potential is ultimately limited by the natural frequency of the use case — you can't turn a quarterly task into a daily habit. 80% of retention potential is baked into the natural frequency of the workflow; companies win instead by expanding into adjacent, higher-frequency use cases. He cites Calm, whose retention spiked when it added a nightly sleep use case alongside occasional meditation.

Relevance: for D2C especially, the question becomes what the higher-frequency reason for someone to come back is, beyond the original purchase trigger.

Key Concept: Retention Drives Everything Else, Not the Reverse

The company with the best retention always wins the category — not the best acquisition, not the flashiest go-to-market. Higher retention flows through to acquisition loops (viral or paid) because a retained customer creates more interaction points to drive those loops.

"Retention Benchmarks" (short essay, brianbalfour.com)

Pushes back on the idea of universal benchmarks. Worth reading before comparing a client's retention number against an industry average without context — low retention can actually be fine when acquisition and marginal costs are low and there are exponential returns to scale for the customers who do retain.

Reforge Program: "Retention & Engagement" (paid)

The deepest version of this material — where the framework above was built out and correlated against real growth data across categories.

Creating a great SaaS product

Creating a Great SaaS Product

Most failures trace back to skipping one of these fundamentals.

1. Start with a painful, frequent problem for a specific buyer

The best SaaS products solve something people already spend money or hours on, and the buyer can describe the pain without you prompting them. If you can't name who feels it, how often, and what they do today instead, the product is still a guess.

2. Get to value fast

Users judge a product in the first session. The gap between signing up and the "this is useful" moment (time-to-value) is one of the strongest predictors of retention. Cutting setup steps usually beats adding features.

3. Build the narrowest thing that works, then deepen

Early on, a tight product for one segment beats a broad one for everyone. Narrow focus makes your messaging, onboarding, and roadmap much easier, and you can expand once retention is solid.

4. Retention over acquisition

A leaky bucket kills SaaS. Before scaling marketing, you want users who stick around, which usually means the product becomes part of a recurring workflow, holds their data or history, or connects to their other tools.

5. Pricing and the business model are part of the product

Price against the value delivered, not your costs. Pick a pricing metric that grows as the customer gets more value, such as seats, usage, or outcomes, so revenue expands naturally with them.

6. Distribution is a design decision

How customers will find you (SEO, outbound, integrations, partnerships, word of mouth) should shape what you build, not be bolted on afterward.

Where to dig in next

  • Finding and validating the problem

  • Product and UX

  • Pricing

  • Going to market

Getting to $1M ARR

Getting to $1M ARR

Product Traits That Speed It Up, and the Metric Games Worth Playing

A practical guide for early-stage SaaS founders: what about the product makes the first million in recurring revenue arrive quickly, and which metric to optimize at each stage.

Prepared October 2026

A note on the numbers

These are general industry heuristics and widely told founder anecdotes, not guarantees. Adjust for your market, pricing, and sales motion.

Contents

1. Executive Summary

Part A: Product Traits That Speed Up the Path to $1M ARR

2. The Nine Traits

3. Trait Scorecard

4. What to Measure Early

Part B: The Metric Games

5. Facebook vs. MySpace: Why the Metric Matters

6. The Menu of Games

7. Choosing a Game by Stage

8. Traps to Avoid

9. Structuring Your Metrics

10. Action Checklist

1. Executive Summary

Reaching $1M ARR quickly depends on two things working together: a product that delivers value fast and sells itself reasonably well, and a team that optimizes the right metric at the right time.

On the product side, fast starters tend to solve a painful, budgeted problem for a narrow customer group, deliver value within minutes or days, replace something customers already do manually, carry some built-in distribution, price in line with value, and retain customers from day one.

On the metric side, the lesson of Facebook versus MySpace is that counting people who showed up (registered users) is far weaker than counting people who got value (active users who reached a meaningful behavior). Early teams should pick one north-star metric tied to value, supported by a few input metrics and guardrails.

The short version

Find a sharp wedge, get customers to value quickly, prove that cohorts retain, then add one distribution channel. Measure value, not attention.

Part A: Product Traits That Speed Up the Path to $1M ARR

2. The Nine Traits

2.1 A painful, expensive problem

Products that sell fast attack something a buyer already budgets for or loses money on: compliance deadlines, revenue leakage, hours of manual work. Nice-to-have tools demand far more selling. A useful test is whether customers would be genuinely upset if you disappeared, and whether they can quantify what you save or earn them.

2.2 A narrow, sharp wedge

Early winners rarely build a platform. They solve one specific problem for one type of customer, for example payroll for restaurants rather than HR software. A narrow focus makes messaging obvious, scope small, and word of mouth easy, because everyone in that niche shares the problem and talks to each other.

2.3 Fast time-to-value

The shorter the gap between signup and the first aha moment, the better conversion, retention, and referrals look. Strong signs include onboarding that delivers value in minutes or days, useful defaults, and imports from tools customers already use. A three-month implementation before any benefit will slow the path to $1M considerably.

2.4 Replacing something painful, not creating a new behavior

Selling against a spreadsheet, a manual process, or a disliked incumbent is far easier than convincing people to change how they work. Products that fit existing workflows through integrations with the CRM, accounting tool, or Slack meet less resistance than those demanding a new habit.

2.5 Built-in distribution

Some products carry their own growth loops:

  • Collaboration or sharing: each user invites others (Slack, Figma, Calendly).

  • Output that gets seen: shared links, reports, or forms that carry your branding.

  • Templates or content that rank in search.

  • Marketplace or integration listings that bring buyers to you.

Even a modest loop meaningfully lowers CAC compared with buying every customer.

2.6 Pricing that matches the value

Founders often underprice. A product that saves a company $50K a year can usually charge $5K to $10K. Higher ACV means far fewer customers: $1M ARR is 100 customers at $10K, versus roughly 1,700 at $50 per month. Simple pricing that a champion can approve without procurement also speeds deals. Many fast starters land in the $5K to $25K range, where deals close quickly but revenue adds up.

2.7 Strong retention from day one

Reaching $1M quickly is not only acquisition, because churn quietly eats growth. Retention improves when the product holds important data, becomes part of a daily or weekly routine, or is hard to replace through deep integrations, historical records, or multi-team dependence. Expansion levers such as seats, usage, or extra modules help too.

2.8 Low friction to buy and to trust

Quick signup, a free trial or pilot, self-serve checkout where possible, and security basics (SSO, SOC 2 when your buyers require it) keep deals from stalling. Early on, reliability matters more than breadth: a few features that work flawlessly beat many that do not.

2.9 A tight feedback loop with customers

Fast companies ship small improvements frequently based on what their first 20 to 50 customers say, and they decline custom work that does not generalize. The product ends up shaped by real usage rather than guesses.

3. Trait Scorecard

Rate your product from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong) on each trait. Any score of 2 or below is likely your biggest constraint on reaching $1M quickly.

Trait Diagnostic question Your score (1-5)
Painful problem Would customers be upset if we disappeared?
Narrow wedge Can we describe our customer in one sentence?
Time-to-value How long from signup to the first aha moment?
Workflow fit Are we replacing a spreadsheet or tool, or asking for a new habit?
Built-in distribution Does usage naturally expose us to new buyers?
Pricing power Is our price a small fraction of the value we create?
Retention Do cohorts flatten rather than decay to zero?
Low friction Can a buyer start without talking to us?
Feedback loop Do we talk to customers every week?

4. What to Measure Early

Metric Why it matters
Activation rate Share of signups that reach the first value moment; the best early signal of product fit
Time to first value Shorter gaps predict higher conversion and retention
Week-4 or month-3 retention Shows whether new cohorts stick or fade
Organic or referral share Indicates built-in distribution and lower future CAC
Willingness to pay How many pilots convert to paid at your target price

If activation and retention are weak, more marketing will not fix the problem. If they are strong, growth tends to follow.

Part B: The Metric Games

5. Facebook vs. MySpace: Why the Metric Matters

The contrast between the two companies is a good lens for choosing what to optimize. MySpace is generally described as leaning on registered users and traffic, which only ever go up and hide whether anyone is getting value. Facebook is widely described as focusing on monthly active users, and more specifically on getting new users to a behavior that predicted they would stay. A commonly told story is the target of seven friends within ten days.

The real choice is between a metric that counts people who showed up and one that counts people who got value.

Metric that counts attention Metric that counts value
Example Registered users, page views, downloads Monthly active users who hit a key behavior
Direction Only ever rises Rises and falls with real usage
Risk Hides churn and weak engagement Harder to move, but honest
Behavior it drives Top-of-funnel tactics Onboarding, product quality, retention

6. The Menu of Games

Several metrics can serve as your early focus. Each rewards a different set of behaviors.

Game What you optimize Good for Example
Activation % of signups reaching the aha moment Self-serve, PLG Facebook's friends threshold; Slack's roughly 2,000 team messages; Dropbox's first saved file
Retention Week-4 / month-3 cohort retention Any product, before scaling spend The flat-line retention curve investors look for
Weekly active accounts Teams active each week B2B collaboration tools Slack, Notion
Revenue per customer Price and plan mix (ACV) Products with clear ROI Fast B2B starters raising prices early
Pilot-to-paid conversion % of trials or design partners that pay Sales-led or enterprise Early B2B firms with 5 to 20 design partners
Customer conversations Calls and demos per week Pre-product-market fit Founder-led selling
Viral loops Invites per user; signups per invite Products used with others Calendly, Figma
Distribution channel One channel's volume Once the product retains SEO, integrations, outbound
Net revenue retention Expansion minus churn Seat- or usage-based pricing Snowflake, Twilio-style models

7. Choosing a Game by Stage

Stage Primary game Reasoning
Before product-market fit Customer conversations and retention If cohorts do not flatten, no growth channel will save you
Retention looks healthy Activation, then one distribution channel Fixing the funnel is cheaper than buying traffic into a leaky product
Approaching $1M ARR ACV, pilot-to-paid, and NRR Revenue per customer decides how fast you get there

8. Traps to Avoid

  • Vanity metrics: signups, registered users, page views, and downloads feel good but predict little.

  • Counting individuals in a B2B product: one enthusiastic user in a company that never rolls it out is not a win; count active accounts or teams.

  • Optimizing the wrong thing too well: if you chase signups, you will get signups, perhaps at the cost of quality. Metrics shape behavior.

  • Running too many games at once: pick one north-star metric and a few inputs that drive it.

9. Structuring Your Metrics

Layer Example
North star Weekly active accounts that hit a value threshold
Inputs Signups, activation rate, time to first value, invites sent
Guardrails Churn, support load, gross margin

Inputs are the levers your team can pull this week. The north star confirms the levers matter. Guardrails stop you from winning the north star at the expense of the business.

10. Action Checklist

  • Write a one-sentence description of your narrow wedge customer.

  • Define the aha moment and the behavior that predicts retention (for example, a count of actions in a time window).

  • Measure time to first value and activation rate for every new cohort.

  • Chart week-4 and month-3 retention by signup cohort.

  • Choose one north-star metric and two to four input metrics.

  • Test pricing: raise it for new customers until you see real resistance.

  • Hold weekly customer calls and log what you hear.

  • Pick one distribution channel to test once retention is healthy.

Build process

Build process

The eight-step formula takes an idea to a build. Each step names the skill that runs it. Say “Hey Cagan…” or “Hey Munger…” and paste the context so far.

  1. Outcome

    What should happen, for whom, and how we will measure it.

    Cagan
  2. Invert

    What would guarantee this fails? List it without softening.

    Munger
  3. Forecast failures

    Which of those are likely, how bad, and what we do about each.

    Munger
  4. Flip the inversion

    Turn each failure into a rule the build must follow.

    Munger
  5. Requirements

    Must, should, later. Each with a user story and an acceptance test.

    Cagan
  6. Design the pages

    Every page in Canva, with empty, loading, error and success states.

    Krug
  7. Interview

    Let Claude ask questions on stack, output format, usability and risk before anything is built.

    Fowler, Krug, Cagan
  8. Build in a fresh chat

    Attach the context pack. One requirement at a time, test first.

    Beck

The build loop

Per ticket: read the acceptance test, write a failing test, write the least code that passes, tidy, run the full suite, open a pull request.

Definition of done

Acceptance test passes. New tests written and the full suite is green. Verified on staging. Edge cases checked. Context file and decision log updated. No stray secrets or TODOs.

Weekly rhythm

Monday, 30 minutes: reorder the backlog and confirm the top five tickets are specced. Friday, 30 minutes: demo what shipped, then ask what slowed us down and change a template or rule because of it.

Operating principles

No side hustles. Nail it, then scale it. Front-load effort, cash or both. Play the better game. Use leverage, supply and demand, network effects and brand. Chase maximum output for the chosen input. Be market-centric, not founder-centric. Lead getters and product come first.

Review rule

No merge without a second look against the acceptance test and the conventions file. AI review is a first filter. A person reviews anything touching money, login or data.

Inputs and templates

Templates to fill in before building. A ticket you cannot write an acceptance test for is not ready.

Outcome brief

One page per product. Copy it, fill it, keep it in the repo.

PRODUCT:
WHO IT IS FOR (one specific user):
PROBLEM (in their words):
OUTCOME (a measurable change):
NON-GOALS (what v1 will not do):
SUCCESS METRIC AND DATE:

Requirement and acceptance test

One per requirement, tagged must, should or later.

ID / PRIORITY: R1 / must
STORY: As a [user], I want [action], so that [outcome].
ACCEPTANCE: Given [state], when [action], then [observable result].
EDGE CASES: empty input, wrong format, duplicate, timeout.

Failure list

From the invert and forecast steps. Attach it to the brief.

FAILURE | LIKELIHOOD | IMPACT | RULE WE FOLLOW TO PREVENT IT

Shared context

AI sessions and new people have no memory. What is written down here is what every session starts from.

CONTEXT.md template

Put at the root of every repo. Keep it under two pages and update it weekly.

# [Product]
What it is: [two sentences, who it is for]
Stack: [language, framework, database, hosting]
Structure: [what lives in which folder]
Conventions: [naming, formatting, errors, how tests are named]
Commands: [run, test, lint, deploy]
Rules: never commit secrets; schema changes need a migration; ask before adding a dependency
Current focus: [what we are building now]

Decision log entry

Log only decisions that are hard to undo: stack, database, login, hosting, payments, data model.

## YYYY-MM-DD: [Decision]
Decision:
Why:
Alternatives rejected (and why):
Reversibility: easy / hard
Revisit when:

Build process

Tooling and access

One owner per tool, and at least two people with admin on anything critical.

Code and branchesGitHub organisation, one repo per product. main is always deployable, work happens on short branches, every merge goes through a pull request.
EnvironmentsLocal, staging and production, each with its own database and keys. Staging deploys on every merge. Production is promoted by hand.
ChecksA pipeline runs tests and the linter on every pull request.
SecretsPassword manager only. Every repo lists its variables in .env.example. Separate keys per environment and per person or agent. Rotate on a schedule, and at once after any leak.
AI toolsChat for planning and requirements, a coding agent for building in the repo, a separate pass for review. Every key has a monthly cap, reviewed monthly.
DesignCanva for pages and the design system. Real content in designs, not placeholder text.
Provider independenceKeep provider-specific code behind a thin wrapper of your own so models and vendors can be swapped.

To fill in on your side: the owner, cost and monthly cap for each tool, and who holds admin.

Code and files

Products

Five software types that work

The 5 Types of Software That Work

For the Full-Booking Machine — mapped to what the market-product research validated as real, underserved need in the contractors/trades vertical (HVAC, plumbing, electrical).

These five categories aren't a feature wishlist — each one traces back to a specific, well-documented pain point uncovered in the underlying market research, and together they map almost one-for-one onto the "Three Core Problems" structure already in the Full-Booking Machine offer document. That alignment is a good sign the product shape is right; what needs sharpening is which market gets it first.

1. AI Call & Chat Answering (Missed-Call Recovery)

The single highest-leverage category for trades. Voice and WhatsApp/SMS bots answer instantly, capture job details, and text back missed callers before they ring the next contractor on the list.

  • Why it matters: industry research consistently shows a five-minute response window often decides whether a job gets booked — a homeowner with an urgent issue who doesn't get an answer will typically call a competitor within minutes, not wait for a callback the next day.

  • What it replaces: voicemail, an overwhelmed office phone, or a family member answering calls between jobs.

  • What "working" looks like: every inbound call or WhatsApp message gets an immediate, useful response — booked, quoted, or triaged — 24/7, including after hours and during peak season.

2. Smart Scheduling with Buffer & Travel-Time Logic

Calendar software built for field service, not generic meeting-booking — accounting for drive time between job sites so the business doesn't double-book across town or run late on every call after the first.

  • Why it matters: paper calendars and generic booking tools don't understand geography or job duration, which is the root cause of overlapping jobs and cascading lateness.

  • What it replaces: manual diaries, shared spreadsheets, or booking tools with no route-awareness.

  • What "working" looks like: the calendar automatically protects realistic travel buffers between jobs and flags conflicts before they're booked, not after.

3. Automated Reminders & Self-Serve Reschedule

Multi-touch SMS/WhatsApp reminder sequences (for example 48hr / 24hr / 2hr before an appointment) paired with a one-tap reschedule link, turning a forgotten booking into a moved booking instead of a no-show.

  • Why it matters: most no-shows aren't refusals — they're forgetting, especially for appointments booked more than a few days out.

  • What it replaces: a single reminder call (or none), and rescheduling that requires a phone call, which is friction customers avoid by simply not showing up.

  • What "working" looks like: reminders escalate in urgency as the appointment nears, and rescheduling takes one tap, not a conversation.

4. Quoting & Estimating Automation

Photo-based intake or structured forms that remove the need for an in-person measuring visit, a templated pricing engine that encodes the owner's judgment, auto-generated branded quote PDFs, and automatic follow-up nudges on quotes that go cold.

  • Why it matters: manual quoting is slow (often a 20–30 minute task that gets deprioritized), pricing knowledge usually lives in one person's head, and warm leads go cold waiting for a follow-up that never comes.

  • What it replaces: hand-written or ad-hoc quotes, inconsistent pricing across similar jobs, and no systematic chasing of unanswered quotes.

  • What "working" looks like: a customer gets a professional, consistent quote same-day, automatically, with a follow-up sequence that keeps the lead warm without manual chasing.

5. Post-Service Retention & Referral Automation

Job-completion triggers that fire review requests, rebooking reminders for recurring-service customers, and referral asks at the moment of peak satisfaction — plus a simple dashboard showing the dollar value sitting in a dormant customer list.

  • Why it matters: nobody naturally owns the follow-up step once a job is marked done, so rebooking, reviews, and referrals happen sporadically, if at all.

  • What it replaces: relying on staff memory to ask for a review or referral in person, which feels awkward and rarely happens systematically.

  • What "working" looks like: every completed job automatically turns into a review request, a rebooking prompt, or a referral ask — with no one needing to remember to trigger it.

A note on validating these categories

The directional need behind each category is well corroborated across independent sources — but be cautious with any single precise statistic (e.g. a specific missed-call percentage or dollar figure) pulled from vendor blog content, since many of those numbers vary widely (one range found: 14–62% for the same "missed call rate" claim) and trace back to AI-receptionist vendors with an incentive to inflate the pain. Use ranges in client-facing conversations, not borrowed precise percentages.

Full-Booking Machine setup guide

Full-Booking Machine: setup guide and Google Sheet fields

You get four files:

File What it is
Full-Booking-Machine-v2.html The app. Open it in a browser (or host it anywhere). It stores its own data on the device and talks to your Google backend.
Code.gs The Google Apps Script backend. Paste into Apps Script.
appsscript.json The Apps Script manifest (time zone and web app access).
SETUP-GUIDE.md This file.

1. Set up the Google side (about 5 minutes)

  1. Go to sheets.google.com and create a blank Sheet. Name it, for example, "Full-Booking Machine".
  2. Open Extensions > Apps Script. Delete the sample code and paste in everything from Code.gs. Save.
  3. Click the gear icon (Project Settings), tick Show "appsscript.json" manifest file in editor. Go back to the editor, open appsscript.json and replace its content with the file provided. Save.
  4. In the editor pick the function setup in the dropdown and click Run. Approve the permissions (Sheets, Gmail, Drive, external requests). Google will warn that the app is unverified: click Advanced > Go to project. This is your own script.
  5. setup creates all the tabs and column headers below, fills in the default settings, generates your two secret keys and starts the 1-minute timer. You do not need to type any headers yourself.
  6. Click Deploy > New deployment, choose type Web app, set Execute as: Me and Who has access: Anyone, then Deploy. Copy the Web app URL (ends in /exec).
  7. Back in the Sheet, open the Settings tab and copy the value next to dashboardToken.
  8. Open Full-Booking-Machine-v2.html. Finish onboarding (or go to Settings > Connection), paste the URL and the token, press Test connection.
  9. In the Sheet's Settings tab, check ownerEmail (alerts go there) and fill in reviewLink. You can also do both from the app's Settings page.

Whenever you change Code.gs: Deploy > Manage deployments > Edit (pencil) > Version: New version > Deploy. The URL stays the same.

4. Getting leads in

Open the app's Speed to lead page. It shows a ready-made HTML form (with your lead key already in it). Paste it on your website. Anything that can send a POST (Facebook lead ads through Zapier or Make, for example) can use the same URL with the fields: action=lead, key=<your leadKey>, name, phone, email, message.

To turn enquiry emails into leads, put a Gmail search in Settings > Speed to lead, for example subject:(enquiry OR quote) in:inbox. The script checks every minute, creates a lead, replies and labels the email fbm-done.

5. SMS and WhatsApp (optional)

Email works with no extra setup. For SMS or WhatsApp, add provider keys in the Sheet's Settings tab:

  • Twilio: smsProvider = twilio, plus twilioSid, twilioToken, twilioFrom (for WhatsApp use your WhatsApp-enabled number).
  • BulkSMS: smsProvider = bulksms, plus bulksmsId and bulksmsSecret.

Then choose SMS or WhatsApp under Settings > Messages in the app. WhatsApp messages sent outside a 24-hour customer conversation need Meta-approved templates, so email or SMS is the safer start. If a contact has no usable channel, the script falls back to email.

6. Limits and good practice

  • Free Gmail accounts send about 100 emails a day (about 1,500 on Google Workspace). Failed sends retry three times, 10 minutes apart.
  • The 1-minute timer uses about 30 to 60 minutes of the 90 minutes of daily trigger time a free account gets.
  • Every message carries an opt-out link. Opting out stops all messages to that person across leads, quotes and jobs (POPIA).
  • Keep the Sheet private. It holds customer details and your secret keys. If a key leaks, change the value in the Settings tab (and the app's token field).
  • One Sheet and one script per client business keeps each client's data separate.
  • Test first: add yourself as a lead, check you get the instant reply, then complete a test job with a short reviewDelayHrs (for example 0).

7. Testing with fake data

A. Preview the app with no backend (nothing is sent anywhere) Open the app. On the first screen click Skip setup and explore with demo data. Or, once set up, go to Settings > Demo data > Load demo data. You get 6 leads, 6 quotes, 5 jobs, scheduled messages and activity, so every page and every dashboard number has something in it. Demo data only works while the app is not connected to a backend. Use Clear demo data to remove it.

B. Test the real automations with seeded Sheet data

  1. In Apps Script, choose the function seedDemoData and click Run. It adds 8 fake leads, 6 quotes, 6 jobs, scheduled messages and activity to your Sheet. Every demo row id starts with demo or DEMO.
  2. Open the app (connected) and press Refresh. The dashboard fills up.
  3. Demo contacts use your own email with a +alias (for example you+demo3@gmail.com), so anything the timer sends lands in your inbox and nobody else's.
  4. Four messages are scheduled to go out about 3 to 6 minutes after you run the seed (a lead follow-up, a quote nudge, a review request and a review reminder). Wait a few minutes and check your inbox. If it is between your quiet hours (default 20:00 to 07:00) they are held until quiet hours end.
  5. When you are done, run clearDemoData. It removes every demo row and leaves your real data alone.

C. Send a test lead through the real form endpoint Use the form code from the app's Speed to lead page on a test page, or send this from any REST tool (a POST to your Web app URL, body type text/plain):

{"action":"lead","key":"<your leadKey>","data":{"name":"Test Person","phone":"0825550199","email":"you+test1@gmail.com","message":"Need a 12 m boundary wall"}}

You should get the instant reply at your +alias address and a New lead alert within seconds, and the lead should show on the dashboard at the next refresh.

Quote tool README

Quote & Estimate Tool Kit

A short quote-request form plus ballpark estimate calculators for trades (roofing, paving, flooring, fencing, painting). Runs on Google Workspace. No monthly fees, no server.

When someone submits:

  • the owner gets an instant email with the lead's details, call and WhatsApp links, photo links, and the estimate PDF
  • the customer gets their estimate by email, with a designed PDF built from a Google Doc template you choose (or a plain confirmation if they asked for a quote instead)
  • the lead is logged to a Google Sheet, photos are saved to Google Drive
  • form starts and submissions are counted in an Events tab, so you can see drop-off

What is in this folder

File What it is
quote-tool.html The form and calculator. One file. Edit the CONFIG block at the top.
apps-script/Code.gs The Google side. Saves leads and photos, builds the PDF from a template, sends both emails.
test-images/ Synthetic test images (one oversized, one PNG) for testing the photo step.
docs/TEMPLATE-GUIDE.md How to choose, edit and add quote templates.
docs/TEST-CHECKLIST.md Step-by-step tests to run before going live.
docs/RATES-WORKSHEET.md Sheet to fill in with the contractor, so no rate is guessed.

Setup (about 10 minutes)

1. Create the Sheet and paste the script

  1. Go to sheets.google.com and create a blank Sheet. Name it "Quote leads".
  2. Open Extensions > Apps Script.
  3. Delete the sample code. Open apps-script/Code.gs, copy everything, paste it in.
  4. Edit the four lines at the top:
    • OWNER_EMAIL: where new-lead alerts go
    • BUSINESS_NAME: shown in emails
    • CURRENCY: 'R' for rand
    • RESPONSE_TIME: must match the page (default '24 hours')
  5. Click the save icon.

2. Deploy it as a web app

  1. Click Deploy > New deployment. Click the gear and choose Web app.
  2. Execute as: Me. Who has access: Anyone.
  3. Click Deploy. Google asks you to authorize. Choose your account. If you see "Google hasn't verified this app", click Advanced, then Go to (project name). This is normal for your own script. It asks for access to Sheets, Drive, Docs and Gmail sending. All are needed (Docs is for the quote template).
  4. Copy the Web app URL (it ends in /exec).

3. Set up the quote design

  1. Back in the Sheet, a new menu Quote tool appears after you reload it.
  2. Click Quote tool > Create starter templates. This makes three Google Doc templates in your Drive and adds three tabs: Settings, Templates and Placeholders. Approve the permissions when asked.
  3. Open Settings. Fill in your phone, email, address, website and company number. Pick your template in ActiveTemplate.
  4. Click Quote tool > Email me a sample quote and check the PDF in your inbox. See docs/TEMPLATE-GUIDE.md for editing templates and adding your own.

If you used an earlier version of this kit, delete the old Leads tab first, because its columns changed.

4. Configure the page

Open quote-tool.html in a text editor (Notepad, VS Code). Edit only the CONFIG block:

  • endpoint: paste the Web app URL
  • businessName, phoneDisplay, responseTime, currency
  • trades: each trade has options with a low and high price per unit, plus a minCharge. Use the contractor's real rates. See docs/RATES-WORKSHEET.md.
  • Leave ratesConfigured: false until you have tested. While it is false, a "demo rates" banner shows and every email is tagged [TEST].

To add a trade, copy one trade block and give it a new key. To remove one, delete its block.

5. Test, then go live

  1. Run everything in docs/TEST-CHECKLIST.md.
  2. Set ratesConfigured: true. The banner and the [TEST] tags disappear.
  3. Put the page on the contractor's site:
    • Upload quote-tool.html to their hosting and link to it, or
    • Embed it in an existing page with an iframe: <iframe src="https://their-site.co.za/quote-tool.html" style="width:100%;height:900px;border:0"></iframe>
    • Free options if they have no hosting: GitHub Pages or Netlify.
  4. Do not host it from a Claude-published link. Those pages cannot call Google's script, so submissions would fail.

Changing things later

I want to Do this
Change prices Edit trades in quote-tool.html. Re-upload the file.
Change the quote design, logo, title or small print Edit the Doc template or the Settings tab. No redeploy needed. See docs/TEMPLATE-GUIDE.md.
Change the alert email, name, or wording Edit Code.gs, then Deploy > Manage deployments > pencil > Version: New version > Deploy. Saving alone does not update the live script.
Change the response time Edit it in both files (page and script).
Use it for another client Copy the Sheet (File > Make a copy), which copies its script. Redeploy, and set that client's email, name and rates. Each client then has their own data and URL.

The Sheet

  • Leads tab: time, reference (EST-1001...), type, name, phone, email, suburb, project, option, size, estimate low/high, notes, photo links, quote PDF link, test flag, and a Status column (starts as "New"; update it as you work the lead).
  • Events tab: form_start, mode_estimate, mode_quote, submitted. Compare starts to submissions to find drop-off.
  • Names that start with =, +, - or @ are stored with a leading apostrophe so they cannot run as spreadsheet formulas.

Troubleshooting

Problem Likely cause and fix
"That didn't send" on the page The endpoint URL is wrong or the deployment access is not "Anyone". Re-check step 2. Open the URL in a browser: you should see a Google error about doGet, not a login page.
Page says "Preview mode: nothing was sent" endpoint still has the PASTE placeholder.
Changed Code.gs but behaviour did not change You must deploy a new version (see table above).
Emails land in spam Normal for the first few. Ask the owner to mark the alert "Not spam". Customer emails send from the owner's Google account.
No emails but the Sheet fills Authorization was skipped or MailApp was blocked. In Apps Script, run any function once and approve the permissions. Check the daily limit below.
Lead arrives but there is no PDF The owner email says why. Usually the ActiveTemplate name is not in the Templates tab, or the template Doc was deleted. Fix it in Settings or Templates, then run Email me a sample quote.
Tags like {{client_name}} show in the PDF The tag is mistyped in the template. Compare it with the Placeholders tab.
"Quote tool" menu is missing Reload the Sheet. The menu is added when the Sheet opens.
Photos missing from the email The photo was too big after shrinking, or the browser could not read it (some HEIC files). The lead still arrives.
Customer on iPhone cannot pick photos Make sure the page is served over https.

Limits to know about

  • Email quota: a free Gmail account sends about 100 emails a day, Google Workspace about 1,500. Each lead sends up to two emails.
  • The estimate is calculated in the browser. The script checks it is sensible but does not recompute it. Fine for a ballpark. Do not use it where the number is binding.
  • PDF quotes and photos live in the deploying account's Drive (folders "Quote tool quotes" and "Quote tool photos"). Links open for that account only. Share the folders if staff need access.
  • WhatsApp link assumes South African numbers starting with 0.
  • Privacy (POPIA): the form collects names, phone numbers, emails and photos of homes. The page states why and that details are used for the request only. Keep the Sheet and Drive folder private, and delete leads you no longer need.
  • The calculator is a ballpark. The page, the email and the PDF all say so. Keep that wording, and think twice before retitling the PDF "Quotation".
  • Each PDF adds a few seconds to the customer's wait after they press the button.

Template guide

Quote design: choosing and editing templates

The PDF the customer receives is built from a Google Doc template. You pick which one in the Sheet, and you edit the look in Google Docs like any other document.

How it works

  1. A customer submits an estimate request.
  2. The script makes a copy of the active template, swaps the {{tags}} for the customer's details, and exports the copy as a PDF.
  3. The PDF is attached to both emails and saved in the Drive folder "Quote tool quotes". The working copy is thrown away.
  4. If anything goes wrong with the template, the lead and both emails still go out without the PDF, and the owner's email says why.

Choosing a template (the back end)

  1. Open the Google Sheet and go to the Settings tab.
  2. In the row ActiveTemplate, click the Value cell and pick from the dropdown.
  3. Use Quote tool > Email me a sample quote to see it, filled with sample data, in your inbox. Do this after every change.

Three starter templates are created automatically the first time they are needed (or on demand from Quote tool > Create starter templates):

Name Look
Bold Colour band header, Montserrat. Suits trades.
Classic Navy rule, serif type. Formal.
Clean Green accents, lots of white space.

Editing a template

  1. Go to the Templates tab and click the link in the Open column.
  2. Edit it like any Google Doc: change colours, fonts, spacing, wording, add your logo, add a signature line.
  3. Keep the {{tags}} exactly as written, double curly brackets and lower case. The full list is in the Placeholders tab.
  4. A tag you leave out is simply not shown. A tag with a typo is not replaced, so it appears as raw text. The sample email will show you.

Adding your own template

  1. Make any Google Doc and put {{tags}} in it.
  2. In the Templates tab, add a row: a name in column A, the Doc's link (or its ID) in column B.
  3. Your new name now appears in the ActiveTemplate dropdown. If it does not, re-select the cell or re-run Create starter templates to refresh the list.

Tip: copy a starter template (File > Make a copy) and restyle that, rather than starting blank.

Settings that change the document

Everything below is in the Settings tab. No code needed.

Setting Effect
DocumentTitle The big title. Default "Ballpark Estimate".
RefPrefix Reference style, e.g. EST gives EST-1001.
ValidityDays Sets the "Valid until" date.
BusinessPhone / Email / Address / Website / Reg Shown in the header and footer. Blank ones are hidden.
LogoFileId Upload a logo to Drive, then paste its link or ID here. Put {{logo}} in the template where it should appear.
Disclaimer The callout box.
NextSteps The "What happens next" paragraph.
Terms Small print.

A word on the title

The automatic document is a ballpark estimate, and the disclaimer says the price depends on seeing the job. Changing DocumentTitle to "Quotation" makes it look like a binding price. Only do that if the contractor is happy to stand behind every number the calculator can produce.

Limits

  • The starter templates are built by script, so they are neat but plain. Expect to restyle one to match the brand.
  • Notes from the customer appear as one paragraph (line breaks are flattened).
  • Each PDF takes a few seconds to build, so the customer waits slightly longer on the confirmation screen.
  • Fonts such as Montserrat and Roboto are Google fonts that Docs provides. If you change to a font Docs does not have, it falls back to a default.

Budget Tracker Pivot Strategy

Budget Tracker → HR, Accounting & SMB Pivot AI hackathon strategy, inversion analysis, judging criteria mapping, and data model 1. The pivot The original product is a budget tracker built for students. The goal is to pivot the same core concept into three adjacent markets: HR, accounting, and SMBs. This document lays out how to avoid failure (inversion analysis), how to win points against the actual hackathon judging criteria, and the underlying data model (UML) that supports AI integration. 2. Inversion analysis: how to guarantee failure Using Charlie Munger’s inversion principle — instead of asking “how do we succeed,” we ask “how do we guarantee failure” — and then do the opposite. Below is what killing this idea would look like, followed by the inverted (correct) strategy. 2.1 Ways to kill the idea Treat it as one product for three markets — keep it a generic “budget tracker” without adapting workflows to how HR, accounting, and SMB users actually think about money. Ignore who holds the credit card — sell to HR/accounting people as if they have discretionary spend, skipping procurement, security review, and IT approval. Skip the compliance/trust layer — no SOC 2, no GDPR/POPIA thinking, no audit trails or role-based permissions, despite handling payroll and financial data. Spread thin across three markets at once instead of picking one beachhead. Ignore existing tools (QuickBooks, Xero, Sage, BambooHR) and why users wouldn’t switch. Price and sell like a consumer app instead of B2B (seats, contracts, invoicing). Never talk to real SMB owners, accountants, or HR people before building. Have no distribution plan — assume organic discovery is enough. Be a slightly-worse general finance tool instead of the best option for one specific, painful problem. 2.2 Inverted (correct) strategy Pick ONE of the three markets first — likely SMB or accounting, closest conceptually to budgeting. Talk to 15–20 real people in that market before writing code to find a specific, underserved problem. Rebuild the product around their workflow and vocabulary, not the student app’s bones. Take compliance and trust seriously from day one if touching payroll or financial data. Price and sell like a B2B tool — seats, contracts, sales calls — not a consumer subscription. Get distribution through channels the market already trusts (accounting firm partnerships, HR marketplaces) rather than hoping for organic growth. 3. Hackathon judging criteria This is an AI hackathon. Technical Implementation (35 pts) explicitly scores AI integration in the working prototype, and Innovation and Creativity (20 pts) rewards originality relative to “common or expected solutions.” Together these two criteria account for 55% of the total score. 4. Mapping AI integration to each criterion 4.1 Technical Implementation (35 pts) This is judged on working code, not slides. Recommended: one strong “hero” AI feature plus one or two supporting features, rather than many half-built ones. Auto-categorization engine — classify transactions (payroll, benefits, travel, SaaS) via LLM instead of manual dropdowns. Highest impact, easiest to demo. Anomaly / fraud detection — flag expenses that deviate from historical patterns, e.g. an invoice 3x the usual amount. Natural language query — “How much did we spend on contractor payroll last quarter?” answered via RAG over the org’s own budget data. Forecasting — simple time-series or LLM-assisted cash flow / headcount cost projections for SMBs (e.g. runway estimates). Document extraction — OCR + LLM parsing of payslips, invoices, or receipts into structured budget entries. Highly visual, demo-friendly. 4.2 Innovation and Creativity (20 pts) The “expected” solution is AI that categorizes spending. To differentiate: Position AI as a proactive advisor, not a passive tracker — flag budget breaches before they happen, not after. Target a specific underserved angle, e.g. AI that translates budget variance into plain English for non-financial HR managers. 4.3 Business Viability (20 pts) Be ready to answer, precisely: who is the buyer, what do they use today, and why would they switch. Judges typically probe this in Q&A even if it isn’t on the slides. 4.4 Presentation and Communication (15 pts) Live pitch. Whoever demos should be able to show the AI feature working in under 60 seconds — a failed live demo costs more than a good slide gains. 4.5 Team Collaboration (10 pts) Every team member should be able to speak to part of the AI integration, since this is partly assessed through judges’ Q&A, not just the scripted pitch. 5. Data model (UML) A class diagram anchors the “AI integration” story to something concrete for judges. The model is deliberately tenant-based (Organization) so it can serve HR teams, accountants, and SMBs from the same schema, with AIInsight as the generic hook for every AI feature. Relationship summary Organization (1) → User (many): employs Organization (1) → Budget (many): owns Budget (1) → Transaction (many): contains Transaction (many) → Category (1): classified as Transaction (1) → AIInsight (0..1): analyzed by Budget (1) → AIInsight (many): receives Design notes: Organization is the top-level tenant — each org sets its own industry, which can later drive vertical-specific AI prompts and rules. Category separates HR-type categories (payroll, benefits) from accounting-type categories (COGS, tax) — this is where the auto-categorization AI feature plugs in. AIInsight is deliberately generic (type, message, confidence) so it can represent anomaly flags, forecasts, or natural-language answers without a new class per feature. Criterion | Description | Max score Technical Implementation | Quality of code, system architecture, and AI integration in the submitted solution, assessed through the working prototype and the codebase. | 35 Innovation and Creativity | Originality of the solution concept and the team’s approach to the business problem, compared to common or expected solutions. | 20 Business Viability | Relevance of the solution to a real business problem and its potential for practical impact. | 20 Presentation and Communication | Clarity, persuasiveness, and professionalism of the team’s live pitch to judges. | 15 Team Collaboration | Evidence of effective teamwork and meaningful contribution by all team members. | 10 Class | Key attributes | Relationships Organization | id, name, industry, planTier | 1 → many User (employs); 1 → many Budget (owns) User | id, role, email | many → 1 Organization Budget | id, period, totalAmount, department | 1 → many Transaction (contains); 1 → many AIInsight (receives) Transaction | id, amount, date, description, source | many → 1 Category (classified as); 1 → 0..1 AIInsight (analyzed by) Category | id, name, type | 1 → many Transaction AIInsight | id, type, message, confidence, createdAt | many → 1 Budget; 0..1 → 1 Transaction

Tool 1 · Objection Response Generator Tool 2 · Expired Listing Outreach Generator Tool 3 · New Lead Response Generator Version 1.0 · 28 May 2026 Design Principles Every tool in this suite follows the same design philosophy. These principles apply to every screen, every component, and every copy decision across all three tools. Before writing a single line of code, internalise these. Core Aesthetic: Surgical Minimalism The design is not minimal because it is lazy. It is minimal because the agent is stressed, busy, and on their phone in a parking lot. Every element that is not helping them get their result faster is hurting conversion. The interface should feel like a scalpel — precise, purposeful, nothing wasted. Typography Heading font: DM Serif Display (Google Fonts) — authoritative without being corporate Body and UI font: DM Sans (Google Fonts) — clean, modern, readable at small sizes Monospace (for generated output): JetBrains Mono — signals the output is a ready-to-use artefact Base size: 16px body, 14px labels, 13px helper text Line height: 1.65 for body copy, 1.3 for headings Never use font weights above 600. Never use all-caps except for small label badges Colour System Background: #FAFAFA (off-white, never pure white — reduces eye strain on mobile) Surface cards: #FFFFFF with 1px border #E8E8E8 Primary action: #111111 (black button, white text) — single high-contrast CTA Secondary text: #6B7280 Success state: #16A34A Border radius: 10px on inputs and cards, 8px on buttons No gradients. No drop shadows heavier than 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.08) No decorative illustrations or icons in the main flow Spacing Use an 8px base grid throughout Section padding: 48px top and bottom on desktop, 32px on mobile Input gap: 16px between form fields Maximum content width: 520px, centred — this is not a dashboard, it is a focused task tool Interaction Principles One primary action visible at all time — the generate button Loading state must be immediate (within 100ms of submission) — show a spinner or animated dots Result appears in the same view — no page reload, no redirect Copy button appears next to the result — one tap to copy on mobile CTA appears below the result — never before it No modals. No tooltips. No onboarding flows. No tutorial overlays Mobile-First Rules Design for 390px width first. Scale up to desktop All tap targets minimum 48px height Dropdown menus use native select on mobile — do not build custom dropdowns Submit button is full width on mobile Generated text box is scrollable if output exceeds 4 lines Tool 1: Objection Response Generator Master Build Prompt Use the following prompt verbatim when instructing an AI coding assistant (Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, etc.) to build this tool. On form submit, call the Anthropic Messages API at: POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages Headers: Content-Type: application/json x-api-key: [USER_WILL_INSERT_KEY] anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 Request body: model: claude-sonnet-4-20250514 max_tokens: 300 system: [SEE SYSTEM PROMPT SECTION BELOW] messages: [{ role: user, content: [DYNAMIC USER MESSAGE] }] Dynamic user message construction: ‘Agent name: {agentName} Objection received: {selectedObjection} Tone: {selectedTone} Channel: {selectedChannel} Generate the response now.’ Display response: extract data.content[0].text and insert into the output box. Handle errors: if API call fails, show inline error below the button in #DC2626: ‘Something went wrong. Check your connection and try again.’ === SYSTEM PROMPT (copy exactly into the system field) === You are a master real estate sales coach and copywriter. Your job is to write objection-handling responses for real estate agents. STRICT OUTPUT RULES: - Output ONLY the final message the agent will send or say. Nothing else. - No preamble. No explanation. No ‘Here is your response:’. Just the message. - Length: 3 to 5 sentences maximum. Never longer. - The message must sound human, not scripted. Vary sentence structure. - Reference the agent’s first name only if it feels natural at the close. - Do NOT start with ‘I understand’ or ‘I hear you’ — these sound rehearsed. - Do NOT end with a question unless it is genuinely strategic. - Match the tone exactly: Confident = assertive and assured, never arrogant. Empathetic = warm and validating, never sycophantic. Direct = short, clear, zero fluff. - Match the channel: WhatsApp = conversational, short sentences, no formal sign-off. Email = slightly more structured, professional close. Face to face = script format, natural spoken rhythm. - The goal of every response is to keep the conversation open, not to win the argument. No preamble rule | Without this rule, the AI outputs ‘Here is your response:’ before every message. That doubles the work for the agent — they now need to read and delete a line before using the output. Remove the cognitive load entirely. 3–5 sentence cap | Longer responses get edited down by the agent, which defeats the purpose. A tight response that handles one objection cleanly is more valuable than a comprehensive essay that requires editing. No ‘I understand’ openers | This phrase is overused in sales training and immediately signals a scripted response to the prospect. Real agents don’t talk like this. The output must sound like a confident peer, not a call centre script. Channel tone shift | A WhatsApp message and an email response to the same objection should feel completely different. The prompt must make this distinction explicit or the AI defaults to a bland middle ground that works for neither. Keep conversation open | The failure mode for objection handling copy is responses that try to close too hard. The strategic goal is to keep the door open, not win a debate. Your job is to write a first-contact message from a real estate agent to a seller whose listing expired with a competitor. STRICT OUTPUT RULES: - Output ONLY the final message. No preamble, no explanation, no label. - Length: 4 to 6 sentences. Never longer. - Structure of the message (do not label these sections, just follow the flow): Line 1: Acknowledge the frustration of an expired listing with empathy.
